newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana's Rawlings heads for poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Ghana's Rawlings heads for poll victory.

text.p: Ghana's populist president Jerry Rawlings, who twice seized power in the West African nation, was on course to become the first leader in its history to win re-election, provisional results suggested on Monday.

With over 60 percent of results in from Saturday's presidential and parliamentary elections, only a late surge by John Kufuor of the rejuvenated opposition's Great Alliance could deny him a first-round victory.
Figures from the National Election Commission credited Rawlings with 54.3 percent of votes and Kufuor with 42.9 percent, based on results from 123 of the 200 constituencies.

In the contest for the 200 seats in the West African gold and cocoa-producing nation's parliament, Rawlings's National Democratic Congress party had 73 and the opposition, which boycotted the 1992 parliamentary poll, 50.
"Rawlings cruises to victory," a banner headline in the influential Daily Graphic newspaper proclaimed.
A spokesman said Rawlings, who has been called everything from a dictator to a messiah, would make no further comment until all results were in and ratified.
"I am counting on at least 60 percent of the total votes to render a second round of no consequence," the 49-year-old Rawlings, who is half-Scottish, told Reuters on Sunday.
In the event of his falling short of an absolute majority, he and Kufuor, a seasoned politician and businessman, will have to contest a runoff within 21 days.
The third contender, surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention, trailed with just 2.76 percent of votes.
The National Election Commission results are being slowly chalked onto a monster blackboard in Independence Square.
"If this trend continues and I lose I will respect the traditional way," Kufuor told Reuters by telephone from his Accra home on Sunday, saying he would congratulate Rawlings.
Ghanaians voted peacefully on Saturday. Election Commission chairman Kwadwo Afari-Gyan estimated the turnout at 70 percent.

Commonwealth and Organisation of African Unity observers have paid tribute to the organisation and conduct of the elections. "We believe that the conditions existed for a free expression of will by the electors," the Commonwealth team said.
Rawlings seized power as an air force flight-lieutenant in 1979, executing three former heads of state. He restored civilian rule but seized power again in 1981.

A former socialist firebrand, he embraced Western-style free-market economics, winning plaudits from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. He made the transition to elected president in disputed 1992 elections.

The main opposition went into the 1992 elections in disarray and boycotted the 1992 parliamentary poll. Against the odds, Kufuor's New Patriotic Party and the People's Convention Party (PCP) formed a common front for this year's elections.
The PCP, which did not exist in 1992, follows the socialist line promoted by Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first president.
Kufuor, who celebrated his 58th birthday on Sunday, polled strongly in and around his stronghold of Kumasi, Ghana's second town and capital of the pre-colonial Ashanti empire.
Political pundits said he appeared to be taking more of the urban vote, with Rawlings winning more of the rural vote.
